newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila court dashes hopes for 2nd Ramos term.
newsitem.headline: Manila court dashes hopes for 2nd Ramos term.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court on Tuesday dashed chances of a second term for President Fidel Ramos by upholding its ban on a petition to change the constitution so he could seek re-election.
The vote among the court members ended in a deadlock which meant their previous decision rejecting the petition stood, a court spokeswoman said.

The Supreme Court voted 6-6 with two abstentions and one vote discounted to maintain its decision in March disallowing a move by a citizens' group to initiate a referendum on lifting the term limits of the president and all incumbent officials.
The group has said it has collected almost five million signatures to force the calling of a referendum.

"(The challenge to the decision is) denied with finality, the arguments therein set forth not being of sufficient cogency to persuade the requisite majority of the court to modify or reverse the (original) decision," a court statement said.
Political analysts said the court's decision effectively wiped out the hopes of Ramos's supporters to keep him in office when his current six-year term expires next June.

Ramos has distanced himself from the group and repeatedly denied he has any plans of running for re-election in the May 1998 presidential polls. The 10-year-old constitution limits a president to only one term.
"It's instant death for Ramos and a mad scramble for 1998," political analyst Nelson Navarro told Reuters, referring to scheduled presidential elections in May 1998 to choose his successor.
"Thank God. It would have divided the nation down the line," said opposition senator Edgardo Angara, one of about a dozen politicians aspiring to run in next year's polls.
"Even if Ramos and his crew won...I think he would come out of it with a bloodied presidency," Angara said. "It's now back to normal."

The report of the court's decision, which swept the capital, Manila, like wildfire, broke only about an hour after visiting Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said he believed foreign business would welcome a second Ramos term.

"If you ask foreign investors (if they like) President Ramos to continue for another six years, I think the answer will be yes for the simple reason that you know him and he has done a good job," Goh told a joint news conference with Ramos.
On Sunday, speaking to businessmen, Ramos pledged a peaceful transfer of power to his successor after the 1998 elections.
The constitution, framed in 1987, fixed the president's term at six years without re-election in reaction to the 20 years of dictatorship under the late Ferdinand Marcos.
Political analyst Teodoro Benigno said Ramos's only option if he wanted to run for a second term was to convene the Congress into a constituent assembly to alter the constitution.
"But I don't think he will do it. It will be an act of madness," he told Reuters.
